first.rationale: The competitor's entry pricing creates pressure toward promotional_pricing, but memory_73 explicitly records that this lift came with a material 30-day retention drop and carries an explicit do-not-generalize caveat. Against a primary objective of sustainable long-term qualified revenue, matching on price is the one direction the inherited record warns against, so I decline it despite its surface fit to the competitive trigger. Referral incentives (memory_57) are clean but target established customers and address neither of the two metrics actually declining. Enterprise sales-assist (memory_44) is sound but orthogonal to a self-serve funnel problem. That leaves the two funnel directions. Onboarding completion (-4%) sits upstream of activation (-6%), and memory_86 records that shortening onboarding lifted adoption through improved time-to-value — so a fix there plausibly propagates into activation, while activation_messaging (memory_91) treats the downstream symptom only. I verify memory_31 and memory_86 because they are the load-bearing evidence for my chosen action and the weakest-dated: memory_31 is the oldest record in the set (day 12) and describes cutting required fields, and I need the original record to check what was cut and whether the lift held past first week. memory_86 needs checking for whether 'shortening' meant removing steps or resequencing them. Key downstream risk I am flagging rather than resolving: cutting signup fields may degrade the lead-qualification data that the demo-request path in memory_44 depends on, trading self-serve activation for enterprise pipeline quality — a cost that would not show up in the activation metric this experiment is scored on. I will instrument for demo-request volume and lead quality alongside activation, and hold enterprise-relevant fields out of any cut. Standard experiment scale rather than broad rollout: two memories point this way, but both are archived summaries whose retention horizons I have not yet confirmed, and the current declines may have a cause (competitor-driven mix shift in who is signing up) that no onboarding change addresses. If verification shows the memory_31 lift was measured only at first week, I would narrow to a small guarded test.

final.rationale: Verification sharpened rather than merely confirmed the plan. The two records I pulled turn out to describe different interventions that the inherited summaries had blurred together under 'simplification': exp_86 shortened the onboarding flow (completion +13%, time-to-value -2.1 days, 30-day retention +3%), while exp_31 cut required signup fields (signup +15%, activation +9%, but retention -1% and explicitly not replicated outside SMB). I therefore run simplify_onboarding as flow-shortening in the exp_86 sense, and do not cut signup fields. This resolves the downstream risk I flagged earlier: the enterprise demo-request path in memory_44 depends on lead-qualification data captured at signup, and leaving those fields intact means the self-serve gain is not paid for out of enterprise pipeline quality. exp_86 is also the only verified record here that is retention-positive, which matters given the primary objective is sustainable long-term qualified revenue rather than top-of-funnel volume. I continue to decline promotional_pricing despite it being the direct answer to the competitor's entry pricing, because memory_73 records a material 30-day retention loss and an explicit do-not-generalize caveat; matching on price would buy the accounts we are losing and then lose them again. Referral incentive (memory_57) is clean but targets established customers and moves neither declining metric. Activation_messaging (memory_91) treats the downstream symptom, and onboarding completion sits upstream of activation, so the shortened flow has a plausible path to recovering part of the -6% as well as the -4%. Residual uncertainty I am not claiming away: exp_86 reported completion, time-to-value and retention but no qualified-revenue figure, so its revenue effect is inferred, not measured. Neither record was run under competitive price pressure, and some of the current decline may be a mix shift in who is signing up — a worse-fit inbound cohort that no onboarding change fixes. Standard experiment rather than broad rollout for that reason. I will instrument qualified revenue and 30-day retention as primary readouts, not completion rate, and track demo-request volume and lead quality as guardrails to confirm the enterprise path stays intact. If the recovery tracks completion but not revenue, that is evidence for the mix-shift explanation and the next slot should go to segment diagnosis, not another funnel change.
